title: Defensible RF/local-sync acceptance criterion for the basement-grade MiniNode
question: What do peer-reviewed 2.4 GHz BLE indoor/subterranean propagation measurements, building-material attenuation data and ITU-R/IEEE link-budget models establish about achievable range, packet-delivery ratio and link margin for a battery-powered node with an internal antenna through masonry, concrete and soil at the MiniNode's intended sites (cellar, shed, garden, workshop), and what quantitative RF/local-sync acceptance criterion (range, RSSI/link margin, packet loss, sync interval) is defensible for the P2 gate without overclaiming whole-house or whole-garden coverage?
why_now: The 2026-10-18 Engineering handoff closes the Gen-0 architecture and makes P2 acceptance depend on 'RF/local-sync performance', but states no threshold. The product is aimed at cellars, sheds and gardens — the worst 2.4 GHz environments — and the first-prototype requirement already includes local radio. Without a measured link budget the gate cannot pass or fail, and the local-first differentiation cannot be validated.
real_world_anchor: 2.4 GHz BLE indoor/subterranean propagation and building-material attenuation (ITU-R P.1238 and peer-reviewed measurement studies); nRF54L15 radio characteristics; ETSI EN 300 328 regulatory limits
novelty_reason: The prior MiniNode topic audits enclosure-induced T/RH lag, condensation bias and reference metrology for the 72-hour P0 run. This gap audits a different acceptance dimension: the P2 radio link and local-sync range. It does not rephrase the metrology question and does not treat RF measurements as proof of the product thesis.
